title: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security
answer: Enablement audits, local models for patient data, device clearance, bias in triage and connected device security.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare is a structured review of how a care organisation selects, deploys and monitors artificial intelligence tools that touch patient care, clinical operations or billing.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are AI systems that run on hardware inside a hospital, clinic or research site rather than sending records to an external service.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device covers any software that a manufacturer intends to be used for a medical purpose, whether it runs on dedicated hardware, a general purpose computer, a phone or in the cloud.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage covers the ways an automated system that sorts, scores or prioritises patients can produce systematically different outcomes for different groups.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Connected medical devices are instruments that hold a network link, whether that is an infusion pump on a hospital wireless LAN, a pacemaker with a bedside monitor, or a home glucose reader that uploads to a phone.

sections.body: This section covers the rules, checks and technical safeguards that surround medical artificial intelligence once it leaves the lab and enters a hospital or clinic. The work here is practical rather than theoretical: teams run enablement audits before a model is deployed, keep patient data on local hardware instead of sending it to outside servers, and prepare documentation for regulators who treat some software as a medical device. Bias testing in clinical triage examines whether a model assigns urgency fairly across different groups of patients. Security work covers the connected devices, pumps, monitors and scanners that share a network with these systems. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, which gives a sense of how much of this work now involves reviewing tools that already exist rather than imagining future ones.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are reasonably settled. Software as a medical device has an established clearance pathway in several countries, and local deployment of models is now a common engineering choice for privacy reasons. Enablement audits have become a normal step in hospital procurement, though their quality varies widely and there is no single accepted standard for what they must contain. Bias in triage is the least resolved area, because fairness depends on which groups are compared and on data that is often incomplete or inconsistently recorded. Connected device security remains difficult, since many devices run old software and cannot be patched quickly. The site lists 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, a reminder that the legal side is still being tested case by case.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader new to the topic should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare, which describes the review process that precedes most deployments and sets up the questions the other pages answer. Local Models for Patient Data goes deeper into the infrastructure choice of keeping computation inside the institution, which matters for privacy and for latency. Software as a Medical Device explains the regulatory category that determines whether a tool needs formal clearance and what that review involves. Bias in Clinical Triage takes on the hardest measurement problem, showing how fairness is assessed when the stakes are immediate and the data is messy. Security of Connected Medical Devices closes the loop by covering the network of pumps, monitors and imaging systems that surround any deployed model. Together the five pages move from preparation, to infrastructure, to regulation, to fairness, to ongoing operational risk.
